Hollywood, 1953. A twenty-four year old Belgian actress arrives from the London stage. Her face is unlike any Hollywood had seen — all cheekbones and enormous dark eyes. Within a year she will win an Oscar, a Tony, and change what beauty means to an entire generation.

scenes.speaker: Audrey Hepburn
scenes.text: I was a war child. I was hungry — truly hungry, as a child in occupied Netherlands. That changes you. I cannot look at abundance without thinking of those who have none. Which is why, in the end, UNICEF matters more to me than cinema.

In her final years, Hepburn served as a UNICEF Goodwill Ambassador, traveling to Somalia, Ethiopia, Sudan, and Bangladesh — places far from Hollywood's lights. She called her humanitarian work her greatest role.

scenes.speaker: Audrey Hepburn
scenes.text: I believe in pink. I believe that laughing is the best calorie burner. I believe in kissing, kissing a lot. I believe in being strong when everything seems to be going wrong. I believe that happy girls are the prettiest girls.
Audrey's path from wartime Netherlands to Hollywood stardom was a journey through chaos and reinvention. Navigate her story to reach the iconic moment...

Gombe Stream, Tanzania, 1960. A 26-year-old Englishwoman with no university degree sits alone in the forest, waiting. For months, every chimpanzee has fled from her. But she keeps coming back, sitting still, becoming part of the landscape.

scenes.speaker: Jane Goodall
scenes.text: I named them. Louis Leakey told me not to — scientists use numbers, he said. But how could I watch David Greybeard and not see a personality? A history? Each face was different. Each one was someone.

Then, on November 4, 1960, Goodall observed something no scientist had documented: David Greybeard was using a twig to extract termites from a mound. He was using a tool. When she reported this to Louis Leakey, he cabled back: 'Now we must redefine tool, redefine Man, or accept chimpanzees as humans.'

scenes.speaker: David Greybeard
scenes.text: [looks up from the termite mound, holding a stripped twig, and meets Jane's eyes with calm recognition]

scenes.speaker: Jane Goodall
scenes.text: We were not as separate as we thought. They felt joy, they grieved, they formed lasting bonds, they waged war on rival groups. Understanding them did not diminish us — it enlarged us. We are not apart from nature. We are part of nature.

Goodall spent decades in Gombe, producing the most comprehensive study of wild chimpanzee behavior ever recorded. Then, in 1986, she attended a conference and saw the data on chimpanzee habitat destruction. She arrived a scientist. She left an activist.

scenes.speaker: Jane Goodall
scenes.text: Every day you live, you make some impact on the planet. You get to choose what kind of impact that will be. I went to the forest to study chimpanzees — and the forest taught me that every life is connected, and every connection matters.

Hollywood, 1962. Producer Alan Pakula sends the script to Gregory Peck. It is adapted from Harper Lee's Pulitzer Prize-winning novel — a story about Atticus Finch, a lawyer who defends a Black man falsely accused, knowing he will lose and doing it anyway.

scenes.speaker: Gregory Peck
scenes.text: I read it in one sitting. I called Alan immediately. I said: this is my father. This is the man I knew. I have to play this role.
Gregory Peck was known for his moral authority — a quality inseparable from his physical presence. He was not acting Atticus Finch. He was, in some essential way, becoming him.

scenes.speaker: Atticus Finch
scenes.text: You never really understand a person until you consider things from his point of view — until you climb into his skin and walk around in it.

Harper Lee visited the set and watched Peck work. Afterward, she gave him her father's watch — the real lawyer who had inspired Atticus. When Peck won the Academy Award for Best Actor in 1963, Lee was in the audience. She said: Gregory Peck is Atticus Finch.

scenes.speaker: Gregory Peck
scenes.text: Atticus made me do the same thing on film that I do in my private life — examine where I stand on things.

Gary, Indiana, 1969. A ten-year-old boy steps on stage with four older brothers. He stops the show. In the audience, Motown founder Berry Gordy watches in silence. Then: 'That kid is going to be a star.'

scenes.speaker: Michael Jackson
scenes.text: I watched James Brown's feet. The way they moved — it was like electricity from the earth was going through him. I practiced until my feet could do what his did. And then I made them do something else.

Thriller — released in 1982 — became the best-selling album of all time. Its 14-minute title-track music video was the first video to transform MTV. The moonwalk, performed live on television in 1983, instantly became the most iconic dance move in history.

scenes.speaker: Michael Jackson
scenes.text: I just wanted to give the audience something they had never seen before. I didn't think about whether it was possible. I thought about what it would look like when I got it right.

Paris, 1981. The restaurant Jamin has been open for three years, and critics are already using words they reserve for once-in-a-generation events. The chef is 35 years old. He will go on to earn 32 Michelin stars — more than any human being in history.

scenes.speaker: Joël Robuchon
scenes.text: I make the best mashed potato in the world. People laugh when I say this. But equal weight of butter to potato, passed through a fine sieve, seasoned with precision — there is nothing more technically demanding in cooking. Perfecting the simple is harder than anything complex.

The Gault Millau guide named Robuchon 'Chef of the Century' in 1989. At 51, exhausted, he retired — an almost unheard-of act in the world of grand cuisine. He gave up everything, vanished from the kitchen. Then, years later, he came back with an entirely new concept.

scenes.speaker: Food Critic
scenes.text: Monsieur Robuchon — why did you retire at the height of your powers? And why come back with these small counter-seats, this informal style? It is so different from your three-star formality.

scenes.speaker: Joël Robuchon
scenes.text: I retired because I was dying inside. Haute cuisine had become theater — elaborate, cold, and distant. I came back with L'Atelier because I wanted to cook at a counter where I could see the guest's face. The best meal is the one you share close enough to talk.

Robuchon opened L'Atelier restaurants in Paris, Tokyo, Las Vegas, London, and Hong Kong. Every one earned Michelin stars. He trained a generation of chefs — including Gordon Ramsay — and changed the vocabulary of fine dining from performance to intimacy.

scenes.speaker: Joël Robuchon
scenes.text: A recipe is only a beginning. The real ingredient is attention — attention to the product, attention to the fire, attention to the person who will eat what you have made. Every plate is a letter. Make sure it says something true.

Villa Fiorito, Buenos Aires, 1960s. The slum children play football in the dirt with balls of rags. One boy never wants to stop — not when it gets dark, not when it rains. His name is Diego. The ball moves at his feet like it is alive.

scenes.speaker: Diego Maradona
scenes.text: When I had the ball, I felt free. In Villa Fiorito there was nothing — no money, no safety, no future. But with a football at my feet, I was the most powerful person on earth.

Mexico City, June 22, 1986. Argentina vs. England. Four years after the Falklands War — two nations whose blood is still up. Fifty-one minutes into the game, Maradona punches the ball into the net with his left hand. The referee does not see it.

scenes.speaker: Diego Maradona
scenes.text: A little with the head of Maradona and a little with the hand of God. That is what I said — and I believed it. The English were angry. But the whole of Argentina wept with joy.

Four minutes later, Maradona receives the ball in his own half and runs. He beats one defender, then another, then another, then another, then another. Sixty meters. Six Englishmen. It was called the Goal of the Century — scored in the same match, four minutes after the most controversial goal in history.

scenes.speaker: Journalist
scenes.text: Diego — two goals in the same match. One by your hand, one by your feet. How do you explain it?

scenes.speaker: Diego Maradona
scenes.text: Football is the most beautiful injustice in the world. The ball does not care who you are or where you are from. I was a boy from the slums. And on that day, I was better than anyone on the planet. That is enough.

Baghdad, January 16, 1991. The Gulf War begins at 2:38 AM. Bombs fall on the city. Every other Western journalist has been evacuated. Three CNN reporters — Peter Arnett, Bernard Shaw, and John Holliman — are live on air from the ninth floor of the Al-Rashid Hotel.

scenes.speaker: Peter Arnett
scenes.text: We can hear explosions. We can see tracer fire lighting up the sky. The city is not dark — it is lit from below by burning buildings and from above by anti-aircraft guns. Ladies and gentlemen, the air war over Baghdad has begun. We are watching it happen.

Arnett had already won a Pulitzer Prize for his Vietnam coverage — dispatches that showed American audiences the war their government was not showing them. In Baghdad, he did something even more radical: he stayed. While other reporters ran, he kept broadcasting.

scenes.speaker: CNN Producer
scenes.text: Peter, the State Department is pressuring us to pull you out. They say your reports are compromising military operations. What do you want to do?

scenes.speaker: Peter Arnett
scenes.text: My job is to report what I see. I'm not here to please the Pentagon or Saddam Hussein. I am here because the people watching CNN deserve to know what a war looks like from the city being bombed. Someone has to be here. I will stay.

The Gulf War was the first war broadcast live on satellite television. CNN's coverage — anchored by Arnett's voice from Baghdad — permanently changed how the world understands war journalism. It created the template for every embedded reporter and every 24-hour news crisis that followed.

scenes.speaker: Peter Arnett
scenes.text: In Vietnam I learned that governments tell you what they want you to believe about war. In Baghdad I learned that if you are in the right place with a microphone, the world watches and cannot look away. That is both the power and the weight of being there.

Cupertino, 1997. Apple Computer is 90 days from bankruptcy. Steve Jobs has just returned after twelve years in exile — ousted from the company he founded. He walks back into One Infinite Loop and finds a company making dozens of products, none of them great.

scenes.speaker: Steve Jobs
scenes.text: I asked every person here: which products do we love? Nobody could answer. We make a hundred things and none of them are exceptional. We are going to make four: a desktop for consumers, a desktop for professionals, a laptop for consumers, a laptop for professionals. That is it. Everything else dies.

In the same year, Jobs launched the 'Think Different' campaign — a tribute to the rebels, misfits, and troublemakers who changed the world. It was not just advertising. It was a statement of identity: Apple exists because the people crazy enough to think they can change the world are the ones who do.

scenes.speaker: Jony Ive
scenes.text: Steve, I've designed something. A computer that comes in five colors, with a translucent shell so you can see the components inside. It looks like it's from the future.

scenes.speaker: Steve Jobs
scenes.text: The iMac. People are going to think we are insane. They expect a beige box. We are shipping a translucent blue teardrop. Good. Insanity is relative. If we are right about the design, it will change what every computer company makes for the next decade.

From the iMac to the iPod to the iPhone to the iPad, each product Jobs launched was built on the same conviction: technology and art are not separate things. The device must work perfectly, look perfect, and feel perfect — because the person using it deserves no less. He was right about almost all of it.

scenes.speaker: Steve Jobs
scenes.text: I am the most fortunate person I know, because what I loved to do and what the world needed turned out to be the same thing. That almost never happens. If you have that — protect it. Do not let anyone tell you it is not practical. The most practical thing you can do is make something people love.
Angola, 1622. Portuguese colonizers hold Luanda and push inland, enslaving thousands. The Kingdom of Ndongo needs a negotiator — and Queen Anna Nzinga will not kneel.
At the peace talks, the Portuguese offer no chair for her. Nzinga signals to one of her attendants, who kneels — and she sits on the attendant's back. She will not be lesser.
The Portuguese break the treaty. Nzinga retreats east, conquers Matamba, and builds a new base of power — welcoming escaped slaves and Imbangala warriors.
For decades she fights on — allying with the Dutch, leading armies personally, and negotiating across three colonial powers. She rules until her 80s, never truly conquered.
She even negotiates the release of Portuguese prisoners, turning each crisis into leverage. Her diplomacy is as deadly as her sword.
Anna Nzinga dies in 1663, still queen, still free. Her name becomes a symbol of African resistance against colonialism for centuries to come.
1236. Batu Khan, grandson of Genghis, leads the largest mounted army in history westward. The Mongol Empire will touch Europe.
Rus principalities fall one by one — Vladimir, Kiev, Ryazan. The Mongol cavalry moves faster than any army before it.
Poland and Hungary are shattered at the battles of Legnica and Mohi. Western Europe trembles. Then — a miracle for Europe — Ögedei Khan dies. Batu turns back.
Batu founds the Golden Horde on the Volga steppes — a Mongol khanate that will rule Russia for 200 years. He rules from his golden tent, dispensing justice and tribute.
He hosts Persian ambassadors, Chinese envoys, and European monks — a cosmopolitan court on horseback.
The Golden Horde reshapes Eurasian trade and politics for generations. Batu Khan: conqueror, founder, statesman of the steppe.
Burma, 1550s. Bayinnaung rises from commoner-born general to king — and turns his eyes on all of Southeast Asia.
He conquers Ava, then Chiang Mai, then Ayutthaya — the kingdom of Thailand. At his peak he rules Burma, Laos, and Thailand simultaneously.
He earns the title 'King of Kings.' But he rules not just through force — he absorbs court rituals, embraces Theravada Buddhism, and unifies cultures.
Trade flourishes. Merchants from China, India, and Portugal fill his ports. He builds magnificent pagodas that still stand today.
His army is enormous — reportedly over a million men. Yet he personally leads campaigns, rides with his troops, and earns loyalty through presence.
Bayinnaung's Toungoo Empire is the largest in Southeast Asian history. He died in 1581 after 30 years of reign — leaving behind a united world.
China, Song Dynasty, ~1040 CE. Bi Sheng, a craftsman, stares at a block of clay. He has an idea that will change the world — though the world won't know his name for centuries.
He carves individual characters into clay tiles, fires them hard, and arranges them in an iron frame. Movable type: each character reusable, reconfigurable — infinite books from finite pieces.
He tests the process methodically — two frames allow one to print while the other is set. Speed doubles. His innovation is also a system.
The Chinese writing system's thousands of characters make movable type harder than in alphabetic scripts — but Bi Sheng organizes them by rhyme category for fast retrieval.
We know about Bi Sheng only because the polymath Shen Kuo recorded his invention decades later. Bi Sheng himself left no writings — just the type blocks, and the idea.
Gutenberg's press came 400 years later. But the concept — movable, reusable type — was first pressed into clay by an artisan in Song Dynasty China.
Rome, 1630s. Francesco Borromini works in the shadow of Bernini — despised by the establishment, yet obsessed with a different kind of beauty.

Where Bernini uses grand columns and classical order, Borromini bends walls into concave curves. His church of San Carlo alle Quattro Fontane fits inside one pillar of St. Peter's — but feels infinite.
He uses geometry — triangles, ovals, hexagons — as the hidden skeleton of his buildings. Nothing is arbitrary. Every curve obeys a mathematical relationship.
His patrons appreciate him grudgingly. He works for the Oratorians, the Sapienza University — commissions he can keep, commissions Bernini disdained.
He clashes bitterly with Bernini throughout his life. Their rivalry becomes legendary — the classical versus the radical, the celebrated versus the misunderstood.
Borromini died by suicide in 1667. But his spiraling lantern on Sant'Ivo della Sapienza, his concave-convex facades, his impossible interiors — they outlived every critic.
Rome, 1620s. The 25-year-old Bernini completes Apollo and Daphne — marble that moves, that breathes, where a god's fingers reach and a woman transforms into laurel. Rome is astonished.
Pope Urban VIII becomes his patron. Bernini is handed the keys to the Eternal City itself — he will shape it for fifty years.
He designs the baldachin above St. Peter's tomb — 30 meters of twisted bronze columns pulling the eye upward into Michelangelo's dome. Theater and architecture as one.
His Ecstasy of Saint Teresa scandalizes and mesmerizes — a nun in rapture, angels with golden arrows, light streaming through hidden windows. It is a complete theatrical experience.
The great colonnade of St. Peter's Square: two arms of columns wrapping the faithful in an embrace. Bernini says they represent the Church reaching out to the world.
Bernini outlives his rivals and his patrons. He works into his 80s and dies in 1680 — the man who made Rome Baroque, who turned marble into belief.
Tangier, 1325. Ibn Battuta, 21 years old, sets off for Mecca. He will not return home for 29 years — and he will travel 75,000 miles, more than any person before him.
After the Hajj he keeps going — Egypt, Syria, Persia, East Africa. Every city he reaches offers a new sultan, a new language, a new wonder. He is welcomed as a scholar everywhere.
He crosses the Black Death in Central Asia, survives storms at sea, and serves as a judge (qadi) in the Maldives and Mali. He collects four wives and countless stories.
India: he serves the Sultan of Delhi for 8 years, nearly killed multiple times by politics and disaster. Yet he survives to write about it all.
China, Southeast Asia, the Golden Horde — he witnesses the Mongol world at its height and its collapse. He meets sultans who remember Genghis's sons.
Back in Morocco, he dictates the Rihla to a scribe — a book that maps the medieval Islamic world more completely than any other document of its age.
Mainz, 1440s. Johannes Gutenberg works in secrecy — mixing wine-press mechanics with metalsmith's craft, experimenting with oil-based inks and hand-cast metal type.
The problem: copying a book takes a monk a year. Gutenberg's press can print 3,600 pages a day. The economics of knowledge are about to change forever.
He borrows heavily from a financier named Fust and pours everything into the Bible of 42 Lines — 180 copies, each identical, printed in two volumes.
Fust sues him before the Bible is complete. Gutenberg loses the press and most copies. He dies relatively poor — but his invention has already escaped into the world.
Within 50 years, presses operate in every major European city. By 1500, 20 million books have been printed. The Reformation, the Scientific Revolution — impossible without Gutenberg.
Gutenberg never became rich. But Time magazine named his press the most important invention of the second millennium. Every book, every newspaper, every democracy owes him a debt.
Korea, 1592. Japan's Toyotomi Hideyoshi launches an invasion with 160,000 soldiers. The Korean army collapses. Only the navy — commanded by Admiral Yi Sun-sin — holds.
Yi has already prepared. His turtle ship — the geobukseon — is iron-plated, arrow-proof, and fitted with cannons on all sides. The Japanese have never seen anything like it.
Battle of Hansan Island: Yi lures the Japanese fleet into open water with a crane-wing formation. 59 Japanese ships are sunk or captured. Korea's southern sea is saved.
He is falsely accused by jealous officials, tortured, stripped of rank. He fights the next campaign as a common soldier — still winning battles.
Battle of Myeongnyang, 1597: 13 Korean ships vs 333 Japanese. Yi positions his fleet in a narrow strait where tides neutralize numbers. He wins — arguably the greatest naval victory in history.
He is killed at the final battle of Noryang — the war won, Korea saved. His last words: 'Do not let them know I am dead.' The battle continued. Korea survived.
Tenochtitlan, 1502. Montezuma II ascends as the ninth tlatoani of the Aztec Triple Alliance — ruler of the largest empire in Mesoamerican history.

His capital city rivals any in the world: 200,000 people, floating gardens, a great market at Tlatelolco, pyramids that align with the stars. Cortés will call it the most beautiful city he has ever seen.
Montezuma expands the empire further south and east, demanding tribute in gold, jade, and jaguar skins. The Aztec calendar stone is carved during his reign — a map of time itself.
1519: Hernán Cortés arrives with 600 men and local allies. Montezuma — perhaps viewing the Spaniards through a lens of prophecy — allows them into Tenochtitlan.
He is taken hostage in his own palace. For months he cooperates, maintaining fragile peace. Then a massacre sparks revolt — and Montezuma is killed, circumstances still disputed.
The Aztec Empire falls two years later. But the greatness of Tenochtitlan — its markets, its art, its cosmic architecture — remains one of humanity's greatest achievements.

Beijing, 1720s. Nian Xiyao serves the Yongzheng Emperor as overseer of the imperial kilns at Jingdezhen. He is also a student — of a Jesuit missionary named Castiglione who is teaching Western perspective.
Nian Xiyao becomes fascinated. Western linear perspective — the mathematics of how parallel lines converge — is entirely absent from Chinese painting tradition. He will change that.
He writes Shiyue ('The Study of Vision') — the first Chinese treatise on perspective geometry, with diagrams, proofs, and architectural applications.

At Jingdezhen he applies these ideas to porcelain design — European architectural scenes painted with geometrically accurate perspective onto imperial porcelain. An East-West fusion of art and science.
The Qianlong Emperor continues this tradition. Nian Xiyao's contribution is to translate a Western mathematical vision into Chinese aesthetics — not copying, but synthesizing.

Nian Xiyao is a bridge figure — court official, ceramics supervisor, mathematician, art theorist, cross-cultural translator. The perspectival tradition he started echoes in Chinese art for generations.
Palenque, 615 CE. K'inich Janaab' Pakal I ascends to the throne at age 12. He will reign for 68 years — longer than any other documented ruler in the Americas.
He begins rebuilding a kingdom that has suffered military defeats. His mother served as regent for years; he inherits instability and turns it into a golden age.
The Temple of the Inscriptions: a nine-level pyramid encoding his life, his lineage, and the Maya concept of cyclical time. It will serve as his tomb — discovered sealed for 1,300 years.
The Palenque Palace — a vast complex with a four-story tower unique in Classic Maya architecture. Astronomers used it to track Venus, eclipses, and the movement of the sun.
The Maya Long Count calendar inscribed at Palenque reaches back 4 billion years — evidence of cosmological thinking that dwarfs contemporary European astronomy.
When Alberto Ruz Lhuillier unsealed Pakal's tomb in 1952, he found jade mosaic mask, jade jewelry, red cinnabar — a king preserved in jade for eternity. History confirmed mythology.
The Inca Empire, 1533. The Spanish have captured Atahualpa, collected his ransom in gold — and strangled him anyway. Rumiñahui, the greatest Inca general, will not wait to be next.
He races south to Quito — the northern capital — arriving before the Spanish. He buries Atahualpa's gold treasure so the conquerers will never find it. Some believe it has never been found.
When Sebastián de Belalcázar approaches with a Spanish force and thousands of native allies, Rumiñahui employs Inca guerrilla tactics — ambushes in mountain passes, scorched crops, scattered forces.
He cannot win in open battle — Spanish steel, horses, and guns are decisive. But he refuses to surrender. He burns Quito to the ground rather than let it become a Spanish trophy.
Captured after a volcanic eruption disrupts his forces, he is tortured to reveal the treasure's location. He says nothing. His silence is the last act of resistance.
Rumiñahui is executed in Quito in 1535. Today he is a national hero of Ecuador — a symbol of indigenous resistance, of a world that burned rather than submitted.
Japan, 1183. The Genpei War pits the Taira clan against the Minamoto. Taira no Tadanori — samurai, provincial governor, and devoted poet — rides to the capital as it falls.
The night before the Taira flee Kyoto, Tadanori rides alone to the house of the great poetry master Fujiwara no Shunzei. He leaves a scroll of his poems — asking that even one be remembered.
The Taira retreat south. For two years they fight a losing war — islands, sea battles, the slow narrowing of a doomed world. Tadanori composes poems throughout.
Battle of Ichi-no-Tani, 1184: the Minamoto attack from the cliffs above. In the chaos, Tadanori is unhorsed and falls into single combat. He is killed — a poem on his person reveals his name.
His killer weeps. Even an enemy honors a warrior who wrote such verse. The poem found in his armor that day: 'As the evening dark descends, I rest beneath this cherry tree — a flower is my inn.'
Fujiwara no Shunzei includes one of Tadanori's poems in the imperial anthology — anonymously, because Tadanori died as an enemy of the crown. The poem outlives the war and the clan.
Tenochtitlan, 1427. The Aztec are a minor tributary people under the Tepanec Empire. Tlacaelel, nephew of the tlatoani, sees an opening — and changes everything.
He engineers the Triple Alliance: Tenochtitlan, Texcoco, and Tlacopan unite to overthrow their Tepanec overlords. It works. The Aztec Empire is born, and Tlacaelel is its architect.
Three times he is offered the throne. Three times he refuses. He prefers the role of Cihuacoatl — co-ruler, advisor, the power behind every emperor. Itzcoatl. Motecuhzoma I. Axayacatl.
He orders the burning of all previous historical records — and rewrites Aztec history, placing their people as the chosen of the sun god, destined to rule. Ideology as political weapon.
He expands the institution of 'Flower Wars' — ritualized combat to capture prisoners for sacrifice. It is brutal, efficient, and keeps neighboring states in a permanent state of military tension.
Tlacaelel lives to nearly 90 — outliving three emperors, watching the empire he designed conquer much of Mesoamerica. He dies peacefully. Montezuma II will inherit the world he made.
